routes.description: Establish that historically meaningful witness traces survived in the Gospel and resurrection traditions despite ordinary discrepancies, transmission, and theological interpretation, and that the total attestation warrants confidence beyond a purely visionary or literary origin.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source proximity and retained local knowledge support substantial continuity, that discrepancies and unusual narrative features are compatible with sincere witness-derived transmission, and that the resurrection evidence resists the proposed ordinary causal alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The combined documentary and resurrection evidence must justify substantial historical confidence in witness-derived traditions without requiring complete inerrancy.

centralBridges.description: Establish sufficient chronological, geographical, and cultural continuity between the narrated events and the surviving accounts.
Explain why contradictions and variations can arise within broadly truthful, independently transmitted testimony.
Show that the resurrection traditions’ content and effects are inadequately explained by ordinary visions or later apologetic construction.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify how the quantity and independence of early attestation should affect confidence in extraordinary claims.
Account for doubt, misrecognition, physicality, and other resistant details as potential traces of unusual experiences.

routes.description: Establish that ordinary historical analysis supports only a limited reconstruction of Jesus and the rise of resurrection belief because the Gospels are late, dependent, anonymous, internally divergent, and shaped by oral transmission and theological controversy.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source relationships and contradictions limit independence and straightforward reliability, that historical method cannot privilege unprecedented supernatural explanations over familiar alternatives, and that visions plus theological reinterpretation explain resurrection belief and its narrative development.

motionBridge.description: The surviving evidence must support only bounded historical claims while leaving bodily resurrection historically unestablished.

centralBridges.description: Demonstrate how dependence, authorship, dating, transmission, and contradiction constrain the Gospels’ evidentiary independence and accuracy.
Apply comparative historical probability to miracle reports without assuming either their impossibility or their occurrence.
Provide an ordinary causal account connecting post-crucifixion experiences, messianic reinterpretation, and emerging resurrection belief.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate well-supported baseline claims such as Jesus’s existence from less secure claims about particular deeds and sayings.
Explain difficult resurrection details through the narratives’ literary, theological, and polemical functions.

sections.title: Documentary Base, Dating, and Historical Proximity
sections.rationale: The identity, relationships, dating, and local knowledge of the surviving sources determine how closely their traditions can be connected to eyewitnesses and the events they narrate.

sections.title: Transmission, Variation, and Gospel Contradictions
sections.rationale: The debate must determine whether differences among the accounts are compatible with broadly truthful transmission or instead demonstrate alteration that materially limits historical confidence.

sections.title: Historical Method and Extraordinary Claims
sections.rationale: The standard used to compare miracle reports with ordinary alternative explanations governs whether strong attestation could ever support a resurrection or other unprecedented event.

sections.title: Experiences and the Origins of Resurrection Belief
sections.rationale: Competing explanations of visions, messianic reinterpretation, missionary action, and the emergence of Christian belief bear directly on whether a bodily resurrection is required by the evidence.

sections.title: Resurrection Narratives: Witness Traces or Apologetic Development
sections.rationale: Doubt, misrecognition, empty-tomb material, physical demonstrations, and supernatural features must be assessed as either resistant experiential traces or products of later literary and theological debate.
